html:
A Buddhist temple in Uji, south of Kyoto, made from a country villa of the Fujiwara regents. The villa was built in 998 for a courtier, Minamoto no Shigenobu; Fujiwara no Michinaga bought it from his widow, and in 1052 Michinaga's son Fujiwara no Yorimichi turned it into a temple. Many at court believed 1052 was the first year of mappō, the age in which the Buddha's teaching would decay, and they turned to the Pure Land hope of rebirth in the western paradise of Amida Buddha.

The Phoenix Hall, finished in 1053, is the one building left from that time. A central hall with two L-shaped wing corridors and a tail corridor sits at the edge of a pond, like a bird with spread wings, and a pair of phoenixes stands on the roof; the name came into use only in the early Edo period. Inside, on a high platform, sits a gilded Amida of cypress wood by the sculptor Jōchō, built of hollow carved pieces joined from inside, a technique he developed. Small carved celestials float on the walls around it, and the doors are painted with Amida coming down to gather the souls of the dying, an early example of Japanese-style yamato-e painting. The hall faces east across the pond, so the worshipper looks over water toward the paradise.

In 1336, in the wars against Ashikaga Takauji, the samurai Kusunoki Masashige set fire around the temple, and nearly all its other buildings burned. A great fire in Uji in 1698 damaged the hall again. It was restored in the Meiji and Showa periods, and the hall and its Amida were named National Treasures in 1951. The hall appears on Japan's 10 yen coin, and the original roof phoenixes are now in the temple's museum. It is part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1994.
